Over the last few decades, public interest in hunger artists has dwindled sharply, and an exhibition of fasting that once filled a showmans pockets would today attract hardly anyone at all. <break time="0.8s" /> There was a time, however, when the whole town took part in the spectacle, and as the fast went on, people came daily, some buying season tickets to sit before the little barred cage all day long. <break time="0.8s" /> Even at night visitors came to view him by torchlight, and on fine days the cage was carried into the open air, where the children above all stared at him in open mouthed wonder. <break time="0.8s" /> To the adults he was often just a fashionable joke, but the children, holding hands for safety, gazed in amazement at the pale figure in black tights, his ribs sticking out sharply, sitting on the scattered straw. <break time="0.8s" /> Scorning even a chair, he sometimes nodded politely and answered questions with a strained smile, or he stretched an arm through the bars so that people could feel how thin it was, before sinking back into himself again. <break time="0.8s" /> Then he would ignore everyone, even the striking of the clock that was the cages only furniture, and simply stare ahead with half closed eyes, now and then sipping water from a tiny glass to moisten his lips. <break time="0.8s" /> Besides the changing crowds, there were also permanent watchers chosen by the public, usually butchers, oddly enough, who in teams of three kept their eyes on him day and night so that he could not secretly take any food. <break time="0.8s" /> This was, however, merely a formality introduced to reassure the masses, for those who understood the art knew well that during his fast the hunger artist would never swallow even the smallest crumb, not even if forced.

Some watchers, however, were careless about their duty, and they would deliberately huddle together in a distant corner over a game of cards, plainly intending to allow him a little refreshment, which they imagined he kept hidden somewhere. <break time="0.8s" /> Nothing tormented him more than such watchers, and sometimes, overcoming his weakness, he sang for as long as he could during their watch, merely to show them how unjust their suspicion was. <break time="0.8s" /> Yet his singing did little good, since the watchers only marveled at the cleverness that allowed him, as they believed, to eat in secret even while he sang. <break time="0.8s" /> Far more welcome to him were the watchers who sat close to the bars and, not satisfied with the dim lighting of the hall, shone on him the electric torches supplied by the impresario. <break time="0.8s" /> The harsh light did not trouble him at all, since he could always doze a little anyway, and he gladly spent whole nights telling such watchers tales of his wandering life and listening to theirs in turn. <break time="0.8s" /> In the morning he was happiest, for then an enormous breakfast was brought to them at his own expense, and they fell upon it with the healthy appetite of men who had spent a long, sleepless night. <break time="0.8s" /> Since no one could watch him every minute of every day, no one but the artist himself could know whether his fast had truly been unbroken, and he alone, therefore, could be its fully satisfied spectator. <break time="0.8s" /> Yet he was never satisfied, and perhaps it was not fasting at all that had made him so terribly thin but his own dissatisfaction, for he alone knew what even the experts did not, namely how easy fasting was.

The impresario had fixed forty days as the longest period of fasting, beyond which he would never allow it to continue, not even in the great cities, and he had good reason for this limit. <break time="0.8s" /> Experience had shown that for about forty days the publics interest could be stirred up by steadily increasing advertising, but after that it began to fade, and a clear decline in attendance could be observed. <break time="0.8s" /> So on the fortieth day the door of the flower decked cage was opened, a military band played, and two doctors entered the cage to take the necessary measurements, the results of which were announced through a megaphone. <break time="0.8s" /> Then two young ladies, delighted to have been chosen for the honor, came to lead him out of the cage and down a few steps to a small table on which a light meal for invalids was waiting. <break time="0.8s" /> At this moment, however, the hunger artist always resisted, and although he willingly laid his bony arms in the ladies helpful hands, he refused to stand up, asking himself why he should stop now, after only forty days. <break time="0.8s" /> He could have held out longer, so why should he be robbed of the glory of not merely being the greatest hunger artist of all time, a title he had perhaps already earned, but of surpassing even himself. <break time="0.8s" /> Then the impresario stepped forward and lifted his arms over the artist, as though inviting heaven itself to admire this pitiful martyr on the straw, and a martyr he truly was, though in an entirely different sense. <break time="0.8s" /> Gripping the frail waist with exaggerated care, he handed the artist over to the pale ladies, and while a meal was fed into the half fainting man, the impresario chatted cheerfully to keep the audience from noticing his condition.
